title: Moon, sun, and the guru
hook: a moon, a sun, a road between, and a real argument about who teaches it
carry: some practices are handed on, guru to student
tomorrow: what color is the lotus at the navel? not the one on the poster.

segments.voice: Yesterday, seed sounds on the petals: in a mantra, the sound itself is sacred. Today, the lines that run between the stations.

A subway map is lines as much as stations. The Sat-Cakra-Nirupana draws its lines too: a moon on the left, a sun on the right, and a road straight up the middle, with the lotuses strung along it. And around those lines sits a real disagreement, one you could still hear today between two yoga teachers sharing a coffee.
screen: `A MOON ON THE LEFT.` → `A SUN ON THE RIGHT.` → `A ROAD BETWEEN, AND AN ARGUMENT.`

segments.voice: The lines are nadis, usually translated channels. Ida runs on the left, linked with the moon; Pingala on the right, with the sun; Sushumna up the center, carrying the lotuses. The Hatha Yoga Pradipika ties a breathing practice to them: in through one nostril, out through the other, then back again, a way of cleansing the nadis. And it stresses learning such practice from a guru. That's a deep Hindu teaching with a name: guru-shishya parampara, knowledge handed on, teacher to student, in an unbroken line. The Mahabharata tells a hard story about it. A young hunter, Ekalavya, asks the great teacher Drona to train him in archery, and is turned away. So he shapes an image of Drona from clay, practices before it, and grows so skilled he outshines Drona's star pupil, Arjuna. Drona asks for his teacher's fee: the boy's right thumb. Ekalavya gives it. Readers have argued over it ever since, and the argument is still alive. One view hears devotion: a teacher matters so much that even his image can teach, so keep practices with someone who can see what you're doing. The other hears a door shut on someone who deserved to learn: the basics belong to everyone. Both honor the same map, and the same reverence for the teacher. They differ on who should hold it, and how it's handed on. The science seat adds one quiet note: the breath is real, whatever a person decides the channels are.
screen: `NADIS: MOON LEFT, SUN RIGHT, ROAD BETWEEN.` · `GURU-SHISHYA PARAMPARA.` · `EKALAVYA AND THE CLAY TEACHER.` · `KEEP IT WITH A TEACHER, OR SHARE IT?` · then, large: `ONE MAP, TWO WAYS TO HAND IT ON.`

segments.voice: Think of one teacher who handed you something you still use. Join your palms, or bow your head a little, and say their name and a thank-you inwardly, the way many Hindus honor the guru before study. If you don't pray, simply hold their face in mind with gratitude for the rest of the sit.
The chakras as a map: its lines are nadis, Ida with the moon, Pingala with the sun, and Sushumna, the road between.
screen: `THE CHAKRAS AS A MAP — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: some practices are handed on, guru to student. One map, two ways to hand it on. Sleep well.

howItsDone: Alternate-nostril breathing, nadi shodhana, is taught in hatha yoga classes; in traditional lineages, breath practices tied to the nadis are learned under a teacher's guidance.

chat.meaning: Hindus have long held that practices are handed on guru to student; Ekalavya's story shows both the reverence and the cost of a shut door. Both sides honor the same map.
